newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Adidas Q2 profit growth hurt by taxes.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Adidas Q2 profit growth hurt by taxes.

text.p: Adidas AG, reaping benefits from increased advertising in North America, said on Wednesday global sales kept rising at a high double-digit pace in the second quarter but profit growth slowed due to higher taxes.

Adidas said second quarter sales surged 37 percent to 1.43 billion marks ($761 million). But net income rose only 20 percent to 69 million marks because income tax payments rose 112 percent over the 1996 second quarter to 34 million marks.

Adidas said the increased tax payments were due to a deferred tax charge of about five million marks in the second quarter and rising profits in high-tax countries, mainly in the Asia-Pacific region and Europe.

The tax bill was also boosted by a conservative stance on using tax credits incurred when Robert Louis-Dreyfus led a group of international investors that turned Adidas around from near bankruptcy in the early 1990s.

Adidas said apparel remained the major growth driver for the brand in the first six months of 1997 when global sales rose 40 percent to a record 3.14 billion marks and operating profit rose 42 percent to 208 million marks.
Apparel sales rose 55 percent to 1.58 billion marks during the six-month period, while footwear sales rose 29 percent to 1.45 billion marks over year-ago levels.

Adidas chief executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus said the order backlog for the group's 13 largest units through the rest of 1997, up 56 percent at 2.44 billion marks, indicated a strong outlook for the Herzogenaurach-based group as it prepares to join the prestigious 30-share DAX index in late 1997 or 1998.
"We see no reason why the second part of the year will not be a reflection of the first part," Louis-Dreyfus told a company news conference.

He said Adidas will keep up heavy promotional and advertising spending, which rose to 13 pecent of net sales in 1997 from 11.6 percent last year, ahead of the 1998 World Cup in France where it will be an official sponsor and in the United States where it has signed a slew of sponsor deals.
Adidas said sales also got a boost from the weak mark against the dollar but warned that ongoing strength in the dollar may start to pressure profit margins in 1998.
"In 1998 we could start to feel the effect of the rising dollar," said Adidas chief financial officer Dean Hawkins.
Hawkins said Adidas has hedged about 80 percent of its dollar exposure at about 1.65 marks, which is well below the current dollar level of 1.88 marks.

Sales in North America, where Adidas has sought to take on global leaders Nike and Reebok in their home turf, grew 51 percent during the first half of the year to 727 million marks as apparel sales rose 93 percent and footwear rose 30 percent.

In other regions of the world, Adidas said sales in the Asia-Pacific area rose 117 percent to 359 million marks as a result of strong organic growth, especially in Australia, and the consolidation of its South Korean joint venture.

Sales in Latin America for the six-month period were up 35 percent to 67 million marks, while net sales in Europe rose 29 percent to 1.99 billion marks from 1.55 billion marks in the year-ago period, with Britain contributing to the growth.

Adidas, best known for its three-striped logo, has poured millions of marks into the U.S. in major sponsorship deals, including one with the New York Yankees baseball team, in hopes of boosting its market share to 10 to 15 percent by the year 2000 from its 1996 level of about six percent.
But basketball shoe sales, one of the largest segments of the U.S. sportswear market and one dominated by Nike, remain a flop as sales fell 50 percent in the first half of 1997.
"We are not performing in basketball where I would like to be," Louis-Dreyfus said.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
($ = 1.877 German Marks)
